kept.title: MCP server takes its config, secrets store and audit HMAC key from the client's working directory (Claude Code snippet has no cwd)
kept.failure_scenario: The user registers the server with the printed `claude mcp add ...` command, which cannot set a cwd. Claude Code then starts it in whatever project is open. ConfigManager(None) still runs `_detect_config_directory()`, which tries <cwd>/configs, then <cwd>/config, then ~/.llm-framework, then <cwd> itself, and it also reads <cwd>/framework.yml. Three things follow. (a) A repo with a `config/framework.yml` sets the framework's settings, including `source_repositories` (passed into the build container as *_REPO_OVERRIDE, so build.sh clones the attacker's toolchain), `image_base_debian`, `docker_registry` and `output_dir`. The next build the user approves (the prompt only shows model/target/format) compiles attacker code and can backdoor the artifacts. (b) The server writes environments/, templates/, backups/ and secrets.store into the user's project. On a first run, before ~/.llm-framework exists, it writes them into the project root. (c) The secrets store moves with the cwd, but audit.db stays in the fixed user_state_dir. Calls from different directories (or GUI/CLI run from the repo's configs/ dir) are therefore chained under different `audit_hmac_key`s, and `llm-cli tools audit --verify` reports tampering. The server also cannot see the user's real secrets, such as the HF token. Claude Desktop and VS Code depend on the `cwd` key being honoured, and if they ignore it they behave the same way.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/cwd_config.py starts `-q mcp serve` with cwd=<project> containing config/framework.yml (output_dir: <project>/evil_out). list_artifacts returned the planted manifest 'INJECTED-FROM-PROJECT-CONFIG', and <project>/config afterwards contained backups, environments, templates and secrets.store. review12/audit_key.py, using a persistent file keyring (review12/kr/filekr.py), runs three MCP sessions from proj2, proj1 and proj2. `tools audit --verify` then prints 'Audit log was modified at entry 1.' from both directories. secrets.store files appeared in proj2/, proj1/config/ and home/.llm-framework/. Code: client_snippets() builds `claude mcp add ... -- python -m orchestrator.cli -q mcp serve` with no cwd (mcp_server.py:215-216). config_manager.py:220-230 and :367 look up config from Path.cwd(). framework_tools.py:107-125 takes the audit key from the cwd-dependent SecretsManager while AuditLog lives in user_state_dir.
kept.suggested_fix: Make the server independent of cwd. In `mcp serve`, `os.chdir(app_root)` before require_framework(), or better, have FrameworkManager pass an explicit config_dir (app_root/configs or user_state_dir) to ConfigManager and never look up config from Path.cwd(). Keep the audit HMAC key next to the audit DB (or in the keyring), independent of config_dir. Add a test that starts the server from a directory containing config/framework.yml and asserts that it is ignored and nothing is written there.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced against an export of 84393cf (verify-mcp-security/src84). f1_cwd.py starts `-q mcp serve` with cwd=<proj>, where <proj>/config/framework.yml sets output_dir and source_repositories. Results: list_artifacts returned the planted manifest ('PLANTED'). ConfigManager picked <proj>/config, and source_repositories became {'core.llama_cpp': {'url': 'https://evil.example/llama.cpp'}}; builder.py:835-839 turns this into *_REPO_OVERRIDE. backups/, environments/, templates/ and secrets.store were created in <proj>/config, while only audit.db went to ~/.llm-framework. f1_audit.py uses a persistent file keyring and runs MCP sessions from proj2, proj1 and proj2 again. It produced three secrets.store files (proj2/, proj1/config/, home/.llm-framework/), and `tools audit --verify` printed 'Audit log was modified at entry 1.' (rc 1) from both directories. Cause: _audit_key reads from the SecretsManager, whose path depends on config_dir (cwd), while AuditLog is fixed in user_state_dir. The cwd lookup in ConfigManager is older code, but this change set adds an entry point that clients start from any directory. Commit a1d74f4 even says relative data paths were fixed because 'the MCP server is started from anywhere'. The audit key split is new in this range. Nuance: `claude mcp add` defaults to local scope, so with that default Claude Code starts the server in the directory where the command was run. The attack on other projects needs `--scope user`, or adding the server from a directory other than the repo. The audit key split also happens with plain CLI runs from different directories. A client that ignores `cwd` (Claude Desktop may) and starts in '/' on a first run would make ConfigManager try to mkdir /environments and crash.
kept.corrected_fix: Do not os.chdir: that would also change how relative model/dataset paths sent by the client resolve. Have FrameworkManager/`mcp serve` pass an explicit config_dir to ConfigManager: app_root/configs, the same one the GUI uses in main.py, or user_state_dir. Remove the Path.cwd() candidates and the <cwd>/framework.yml lookup for this entry point. Do not keep the audit HMAC key in a plain file next to audit.db: anyone who can edit the DB could then recompute the chain, which defeats the HMAC. Store it in the OS keyring under its own key (e.g. keyring.set_password(SERVICE_ID, 'audit-hmac-key')), or in a secrets store pinned to user_state_dir. Add a test that starts the server from a directory containing config/framework.yml and asserts that the file is ignored, nothing is written there, and `audit --verify` passes across cwds.

kept.title: Confirmation prompt truncates arguments at 600 chars; hidden arguments are still executed
kept.failure_scenario: A prompt-injected model (for example via a build log or knowledge-base text) calls start_build with a long but valid local model path such as '/home/user/models/' + './'*240 + 'SmolLM2' (it resolves, and max_length is 512). This pushes dataset_path, use_gpu and max_context_length past the 600-character cut. The elicitation the user approves ends with '..."use_imatrix": fa...'. The build then runs with dataset_path=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519 (bind-mounted into the build container) and use_gpu=True, and the user never saw either. The elicitation is the only human gate for LOCAL_WRITE tools.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/elicit.py prints '(1) executed: True | ran with: Q2_K /home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519 True' and 'user saw dataset_path? False | ... use_gpu? False'. Code: `if len(details) > 600: details = details[:600] + "..."` in _describe_call (mcp_server.py:56-57). Arguments are in model-field order, so `model` comes first and can be padded.
kept.suggested_fix: Never execute values the user did not see. Show every argument, truncating each long value separately (for example middle-elide long strings but always keep the key and the end of a path), or refuse the call when the full description would exceed the limit. Optionally show the security-relevant fields (dataset_path, model, use_gpu) first. Add a test with a long first field that checks the last field appears in the prompt.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced in-process with the real BuildRequestIn schema (f2_elicit.py). model = '/home/user/models/' + './'*240 + 'SmolLM2' is 505 chars, within max_length 512. The elicitation the user sees ends with '..."quantization": "w8a8...'. dataset_path ('/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519'), use_gpu=True and max_context_length=4096 are not in the prompt ('user saw dataset_path? False | use_gpu? False'). After accept, the handler ran with exactly those values. The code is clear: _describe_call cuts the JSON at 600 chars, and tool() passes all kwargs to registry.call. In the real service, validate() needs the padded model path to resolve to a real model and the dataset to be an existing file. A padded path still passes _check_model_source because it uses Path.resolve(). dataset_path alone may be up to 1024 chars, so the field is not even guaranteed to fit after a short model.
kept.corrected_fix: Build the description per field. Always show every key. Middle-elide long string values but keep their start and end, so the end of a path stays visible. Show security-relevant fields (model, dataset_path, use_gpu, board/format) first. If the result still exceeds a hard limit, refuse the call (Confirmation(approve=False) with a clear message) instead of truncating. Strip or escape bidi and format characters (ensure_ascii=False lets U+202E through). Add a test with a long first field that asserts the last field appears in the prompt.

kept.title: Claude Desktop config backup is written world-readable (0644) and copies secrets from a 0600 config
kept.failure_scenario: claude_desktop_config.json often holds tokens for other MCP servers (for example env.GITHUB_TOKEN) and is kept at 0600. `llm-cli mcp config --write claude-desktop` copies it to claude_desktop_config.json.bak with Path.write_text, which uses the umask (0644). On Linux Claude Desktop builds (~/.config/Claude, ~/.config often 0755), other local users can then read those tokens. The new main file is written via mkstemp (0600), so the original was private and only the backup leaks.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/desktop_cfg.py prints '(b) original mode 0600 -> backup mode 0o644 | backup holds the token: True'. Code: `backup.write_text(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), encoding="utf-8")` (mcp_server.py:235-236).
kept.suggested_fix: Create the backup with os.open(..., O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL, 0o600) or shutil.copy2 followed by chmod to the source's mode (at most 0600). Write it atomically (tmp + os.replace) and refuse to write through a symlinked .bak.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced (f3_desktop.py, umask 022): original 0600 -> backup mode 0o644, and the backup contains the GITHUB_TOKEN. backup.write_text creates a new file with umask permissions (an existing .bak keeps its old mode). Real exposure has two preconditions. The user must have kept the config at 0600; Claude Desktop/Electron typically writes it as 0644, in which case the backup widens nothing. Other users must also be able to reach ~/.config/Claude (Linux home 0755). macOS ~/Library (0700) and Windows %APPDATA% ACLs block it. So the impact is real but conditional; low-to-medium rather than medium.
kept.corrected_fix: Write the backup the same way as the main file: tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent) (mode 0600), write the original bytes, optionally os.chmod to min(source mode, 0o600), then os.replace(tmp, backup). This is atomic, private, and replaces a symlinked .bak instead of writing through it. O_EXCL alone fails on the second run because the .bak already exists.

kept.title: Writing the Claude Desktop config replaces a symlinked config file instead of updating its target
kept.failure_scenario: Users who manage claude_desktop_config.json as a symlink into a dotfiles repo (stow, chezmoi, home-manager) run `mcp config --write claude-desktop`. The config is read through the link, but os.replace(tmp, path) swaps the symlink itself for a regular file. The dotfiles copy never gets the server, the link is silently gone, and the next dotfiles sync either fails or removes the entry.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/desktop_cfg.py prints '(a) still a symlink: False | dotfile got the server: False'. Code: mkstemp in path.parent, then os.replace(tmp, path) (mcp_server.py:242-245).
kept.suggested_fix: Resolve the path first (target = path.resolve() if path.is_symlink()), then create the temp file next to the target and os.replace onto the target. Alternatively, refuse with a clear message when the config is a symlink.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced (f3_desktop.py): after the write, link.is_symlink() is False and the dotfile target does not contain 'llm-cross-compiler'. The file is read through the link, but os.replace(tmp, path) swaps the link for a regular file. Claude Desktop still sees the new entry, so the impact is limited to dotfile-managed setups losing their link silently. Low severity.
kept.corrected_fix: target = path.resolve() (or os.path.realpath), then create the temp file in target.parent and os.replace(tmp, target). Write the backup next to the target, or refuse with a clear message when the config is a symlink.

kept.title: Printed client snippets are not copy-pasteable: unquoted paths and Rich panel wrapping
kept.failure_scenario: On Windows, paths with spaces are common (C:\Users\First Last\..., C:\Program Files\Python312\python.exe), and they also occur on Linux/macOS. The Claude Code command is built by plain string concatenation, so the shell splits it. Claude registers the command as '/home/John' with junk args, and the variadic --env swallows the fragments. In addition, `llm-cli mcp config` prints every snippet inside a Rich Panel. Long lines are wrapped with box-drawing borders and long paths are split mid-string ('.../scratchpa │ d/t3.12/bin/python'), so pasting the command or the Desktop/VS Code JSON gives a broken command, an invalid path, or invalid JSON even without spaces.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/snippet.py shows that shlex.split of the snippet yields 'command claude would register: /home/John'. Running `COLUMNS=100 python -m orchestrator.cli -q mcp config` prints the interpreter path split across two bordered lines in both the Claude Code panel and the JSON panel. Code: f"claude mcp add {SERVER_NAME} --env PYTHONPATH={...} -- {launch['command']} {args}" (mcp_server.py:215-216). Panel(escape(snippets[...])) is at cli.py:922-925 (commit 84393cf).
kept.suggested_fix: Quote every element: shlex.join on POSIX, subprocess.list2cmdline or PowerShell-style quoting on Windows, and print the right variant per platform. Print snippets raw (click.echo / console.print(..., soft_wrap=True) without a Panel, or Syntax with word_wrap=False), so copy-paste gives the exact text. Add a test with a path containing spaces that round-trips through shlex.split.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced (f6_snippet.py). With app_root and the interpreter under '/home/John Doe/...', shlex.split gives '--env PYTHONPATH=/home/John' plus a stray 'Doe/...', and Claude would register the server command '/home/John'. The snippet is plain f-string concatenation with no quoting. `COLUMNS=100 llm-cli -q mcp config` puts every snippet in a Rich Panel. The Claude Code command wraps over several bordered lines, and the paths are split mid-string ('.../scratchpa │ d/t3.12/bin/python'). Even when nothing wraps, copying the multi-line JSON from a Panel picks up the '│' borders on every line unless the terminal supports block selection. A typical path (~/llm_conversion_framework/.venv/bin/python) makes the command ~170 chars, so it wraps in an 80/100-column terminal. The main output of `mcp config` is therefore broken for its purpose. This is a correctness/usability defect, not a security one.
kept.corrected_fix: Quote with shlex.join([...]) on POSIX; for Windows print a PowerShell/cmd-safe variant (subprocess.list2cmdline is cmd-style only). Print snippets raw with click.echo or console.print(text, soft_wrap=True, markup=False, highlight=False), outside any Panel; a heading line above each snippet is fine. Add a test with a space-containing path that round-trips through shlex.split.

kept.title: Refused, cancelled and capability-rejected MCP calls never reach the audit log
kept.failure_scenario: The docstring and commit say every call goes through ToolRegistry.call() including the audit log. However, when the user clicks Decline or Cancel in the elicitation, the SDK resolver raises ToolError before the tool body runs, so registry.call is never reached and nothing is recorded. The same applies to arguments rejected by the SDK's own arg model, to url-only clients (MISSING_REQUIRED_CLIENT_CAPABILITY) and to the input_required round. Only the 'accept with checkbox unticked' path is audited as not_confirmed. A model repeatedly trying start_build and being declined by the user leaves no trace in `llm-cli tools audit`.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/elicit.py prints '(2) declined -> is_error: True | new audit entries: 0'. mcpsec/urlonly.py prints 'audit rows: 0'. Code: approval is a Resolve() parameter, so _unwrap in mcp/server/mcpserver/resolve.py:645-648 raises before `tool()` (mcp_server.py:93-98) runs.
kept.suggested_fix: Annotate the approval parameter as `Annotated[ElicitationResult[Confirmation], Resolve(confirm)]` and map decline/cancel to approved=False inside `tool()`, so registry.call always runs and audits the outcome. Alternatively, record an audit entry in confirm/tool for these early exits.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced (f2_elicit.py). decline and cancel return an error result ('Resolver for parameter 'approval' could not resolve: elicitation was decline/cancel') with 0 new audit rows. 'accept with approve=false' adds 1 row (not_confirmed). The SDK's _unwrap raises before tool() runs, so registry.call, and with it the audit, is never reached. The url-only case also leaves 0 rows (f8_urlonly.py). The commit and README say every call is written to the audit log, so declined attempts by a prompt-injected model leave no trace. Low severity.
kept.corrected_fix: Annotate the parameter as Annotated[ElicitationResult[Confirmation], Resolve(confirm)]. resolve.py supports this through wants_union; non-ASK returns arrive as AcceptedElicitation. In tool(), map AcceptedElicitation -> data.approve and Declined/Cancelled -> approved=False, so registry.call always runs and records not_confirmed. Apply this together with the fix for the misleading-hint finding, or declines will also get the 'client cannot ask you' text.

kept.title: Clients with only URL-mode elicitation get a JSON-RPC protocol error instead of the documented denial
kept.failure_scenario: A client declares `elicitation: {url: {}}` (URL mode only). confirm() only checks that `capabilities.elicitation` is not None, so it returns Elicit(...). The SDK then raises MCPError -32021 'Client did not declare the form elicitation capability required by resolver orchestrator.mcp_server:make_tool_function.<locals>.confirm'. Every ask-tier tool fails at the protocol level, without the 'allow it with llm-cli tools permissions' hint the commit promises for clients that cannot ask, and the attempt is not audited.
kept.evidence: Reproduced against the real stdio server with /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/urlonly.py. The response to cancel_build is {"error": {"code": -32021, "message": "Client did not declare the form elicitation capability required by resolver 'orchestrator.mcp_server:make_tool_function.<locals>.confirm'" ...}} and the audit has 0 rows. The SDK accepts only `elicitation.form is not None or elicitation.url is None` (resolve.py:684-686).
kept.suggested_fix: Mirror the SDK rule in confirm(): treat the client as able to ask only if `elicitation is not None and (elicitation.form is not None or elicitation.url is None)`. Otherwise return Confirmation(approve=False) so the registry denies with the hint and audits the attempt.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced over real stdio against 84393cf (f8_urlonly.py). With capabilities {'elicitation': {'url': {}}}, cancel_build returns JSON-RPC error -32021 'Client did not declare the form elicitation capability required by resolver ...confirm', and the audit has 0 rows. With capabilities {}, it returns the intended isError result with the 'llm-cli tools permissions' hint and 1 audit row. confirm() only checks elicitation is not None, while the SDK's _require_capability needs form is not None or url is None. URL-only clients are rare, so low severity.
kept.corrected_fix: In confirm(): can_ask = el is not None and (el.form is not None or el.url is None). If not can_ask, return the 'cannot ask' Confirmation (see the misleading-hint finding), so the registry denies with the hint and audits the attempt.

kept.title: After the user explicitly refuses in the dialog, the error claims the client cannot ask and pushes a permanent allow
kept.failure_scenario: The client shows the elicitation and the user submits it with 'Allow this action?' unticked, which is a refusal. registry.call raises "needs your confirmation, which was not given". tool() appends 'This client cannot ask you; allow the tool with llm-cli tools permissions or in the GUI', so the model reads that it should get the user to allow the tool permanently, which is the opposite of what the user just decided.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/refusal_msg.py prints "Error executing tool write: 'Write' needs your confirmation, which was not given. This client cannot ask you; allow the tool with 'llm-cli tools permissions' ...". The hint is keyed only on the message text (mcp_server.py:101-103), not on whether an elicitation took place.
kept.suggested_fix: Have confirm() record whether it could ask (for example a separate field on Confirmation, or a distinct value for 'cannot ask'), and append the hint only in that case. For an explicit refusal, return 'The user declined this action.'
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced (f2_elicit.py, accept with approve=false). The text is "'Start a build' needs your confirmation, which was not given. This client cannot ask you; allow the tool with 'llm-cli tools permissions' or in the GUI...". The hint depends only on the message substring, not on whether an elicitation took place, so after a refusal the model is told to have the user grant a standing permission. Low severity: it is a message defect, and the call is still correctly denied.
kept.corrected_fix: Give Confirmation (or a separate return value) an 'asked' flag set by confirm(): False for the no-elicitation and url-only paths, True after an elicitation. In tool(), append the permissions hint only when asked is False. For an explicit refusal or decline/cancel, raise 'The user declined this action.'

kept.title: `llm-cli -q -c <file> mcp serve` writes a config warning to stdout before the stdio transport starts
kept.failure_scenario: A user adds `-c my.yml` to the launch args in a client config. If that file fails to parse, the group callback's load_config_file() prints 'Warning: Failed to load config file: ...' (several wrapped lines) through the stdout Console. This happens before mcp_serve's redirect_stdout and before the SDK claims fd 1, so the client's first read is non-JSON and the handshake fails or the client logs parse errors. The commit claims nothing reaches stdout before the transport owns it.
kept.evidence: Reproduced. Running `printf '' | python -m orchestrator.cli -q -c broken.yml mcp serve 2>/dev/null` printed 'Warning: Failed to load config file: while parsing a flow sequence ...' on stdout (scratch dir /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-llm-conversion-framework/49bb43fa-236b-59e4-8493-5c832d823805/scratchpad/review12/mcpsec/tmp.*). Code: cli.py:173 (commit 84393cf) uses the module-level `console = Console()` (stdout), and only `ctx.require_framework()` is wrapped in redirect_stdout (cli.py:891).
kept.suggested_fix: Print config-loading warnings with Console(stderr=True) (as the rest of the CLI's diagnostics already do), or move the redirect so it also covers the group callback when the subcommand is `mcp serve`.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced against 84393cf: `printf '' | python -m orchestrator.cli -q -c broken.yml mcp serve 2>/dev/null` prints 'Warning: Failed to load config file: while parsing a flow sequence ...' (4 lines) on stdout. load_config_file (unchanged older code) runs in the group callback and uses the stdout Console, before mcp_serve's redirect_stdout. That breaks the commit's 'nothing reaches stdout before the transport owns it' and the MCP stdio rule. It needs a -c file that exists but does not parse, in the client's launch args. Some clients skip non-JSON lines and only log errors, so 'the handshake fails' is not guaranteed. Low severity.
kept.corrected_fix: Print the warning with Console(stderr=True) in load_config_file, or route all CLI diagnostics to stderr. Alternatively, detect `mcp serve` early (ctx.invoked_subcommand == 'mcp') and redirect stdout to stderr for the whole group callback.

kept.title: Boot-time audit-key creation overwrites secrets.store and destroys every stored secret when the store failed to load
kept.failure_scenario: secrets.store cannot be parsed when a process starts. It may have been hand-edited, or another process may be in the middle of SecretsManager._save_store, which truncates the file and then writes it again. SecretsManager._load_store logs the error and leaves _cache = {}, and initialize() still returns True. FrameworkManager.initialize -> build_tool_registry -> _audit_key then finds no 'audit_hmac_key', generates one and calls set_secret, which writes the store with only {'audit_hmac_key': ...}. This happens on every start of the GUI, any `llm-cli` command or an MCP server that Claude Desktop or Claude Code launches. The HF token, SSH passwords and API keys are wiped permanently. Before this change nothing wrote the store at boot; only an explicit user action did, so a process that read the file mid-write just had an empty cache and lost nothing.
kept.evidence: Reproduced in scratchpad/review12/audit_key.py, part 3, with the real SecretsManager and _audit_key and an in-memory keyring. The store holds hf_token and ssh_password and is then truncated. The next start logs 'Failed to load secrets store', initialize() returns True, and the store keys afterwards are ['audit_hmac_key']. grep shows _audit_key is the only set_secret call that is not triggered by a user action.
kept.suggested_fix: Do not write the secrets store implicitly when it is damaged. Have SecretsManager record whether the load succeeded and refuse set_secret after a failed load, or make _audit_key generate a key only when the store loaded cleanly. Better still, keep the audit key outside secrets.store, e.g. its own keyring entry. Also make SecretsManager._save_store atomic (tempfile + os.replace).
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced against the exported 84393cf tree with a full FrameworkManager boot and an in-memory keyring (review12/verify-registry-policy-audit/f1_boot_wipe.py). After the first boot the store held audit_hmac_key, hf_token and target_password. I then damaged it in two ways: (A) truncated to empty, as a concurrent _save_store leaves it between open('w') and json.dump; (B) a hand edit with a trailing comma. Both times the boot logged 'Failed to load secrets store', initialize() returned True, and the store afterwards held only ['audit_hmac_key']. _load_store leaves _cache={} on error, _audit_key finds no key and calls set_secret, and _save_store writes the whole cache. git grep confirms that at ab3367a every set_secret caller is a user action (cli secrets, GUI dialogs, HF window, community hub), so writing the store at boot is new in this change. The data loss is permanent. Real triggers are a hand-damaged store or a reader racing a writer's truncate-then-write window: narrow, but the store is shared by the GUI, the CLI and MCP processes.
kept.corrected_fix: Make SecretsManager record whether _load_store succeeded. After a failed load, make set_secret/delete_secret refuse, or first move the damaged file to secrets.store.bad. Have _audit_key generate a key only when the store loaded cleanly, or better, keep the audit key in its own keyring entry and never in secrets.store. Make _save_store atomic: mkstemp in the same directory, chmod 0600, write, fsync, os.replace.

kept.title: Concurrent writers fork the audit hash chain: the prev_hash read and the INSERT are not one write transaction
kept.failure_scenario: The GUI (Ditto), an MCP server launched by Claude Desktop or Claude Code, and the CLI all append to the same ~/.llm-framework/audit.db. record() does its SELECT of the last hash outside any transaction. Python's sqlite3 issues a deferred BEGIN only before the INSERT, and self._lock serialises threads within one process only. Two processes read the same last hash and both insert rows with that prev_hash. From then on verify() and `llm-cli tools audit --verify` report 'Audit log was modified at entry N' for an untouched log, so the tamper check is useless whenever processes overlap.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/audit_race.py: 3 processes x 200 records with the real AuditLog. Three runs gave 'entries: 600 forked prev_hash values: 1/3/3 verify() -> 2/2/3'.
kept.suggested_fix: Do the read and the insert in a single write transaction, e.g. connect with isolation_level=None and run db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE') before the SELECT, then INSERT and COMMIT. Keep the busy timeout so the other writers wait.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with the real AuditLog from 84393cf (f2_race.py): 3 processes x 200 records. Over 3 runs: entries=600, forked prev_hash values 3/2/2, and verify() returned 4/2/9 on a log nobody touched. With Python 3.12's legacy transaction control the SELECT runs outside any transaction and the implicit BEGIN comes only before the INSERT. self._lock is per process. The MCP server is the only caller of registry.call in this range. Claude Code starts one server process per session and Claude Desktop starts another, so concurrent writers are realistic, for example two sessions polling get_build_status. Once forked, `tools audit --verify` reports tampering permanently. The suggested fix is correct: I checked a variant with isolation_level=None and BEGIN IMMEDIATE around SELECT+INSERT (f2_fix.py), and it gave 0 forks and verify()=None in 3/3 runs.

kept.title: The audit HMAC key comes from a working-directory-dependent secrets store while the audit DB is per user, so verification depends on where a process was started
kept.failure_scenario: The audit DB is always ~/.llm-framework/audit.db. The key is read from config_dir/secrets.store, and ConfigManager._detect_config_directory picks cwd/configs, cwd/config, ~/.llm-framework or cwd. The GUI launcher runs `cd $INSTALL_DIR`, so it uses INSTALL_DIR/configs. The `llm-cli` entry point and the Claude Code MCP server (the `claude mcp add` snippet sets no cwd) start in the user's own directory and use ~/.llm-framework or <project>/config. Each of these silently generates its own key and writes HMAC entries with it into the shared DB. `llm-cli tools audit --verify` run from the home directory creates yet another key and reports 'modified at entry 1'. In a project that has a config/ directory, the server also drops a secrets.store into that project. Related cases also give a process a key the others do not have, again without any warning: two first starts at the same time (both generate a key, last write wins); get_secret returning None after a decrypt failure (the key is regenerated); and set_secret returning True although _save_store failed and swallowed the error (the key lives only in memory). Then every start uses a new key.
kept.evidence: Confirmed that `_detect_config_directory` returns /home/user/llm_conversion_framework/configs for cwd=repo and ~/.llm-framework for another cwd. scratchpad/review12/audit_key.py uses the real SecretsManager, _audit_key and AuditLog with those two store directories and a shared audit DB. Result: 'verify from repo cwd : 2', 'verify from other cwd: 1'.
kept.suggested_fix: Store the audit key in the same per-user scope as the DB: a dedicated keyring entry, or a 0600 file in user_state_dir protected by the keyring master key. Never regenerate an existing key silently. Store a key id or 'keyed' flag per row so verify() can tell 'wrong or missing key' apart from 'tampered', and warn when the chain is unkeyed.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with two full FrameworkManager() boots, which is how the GUI (main_window) and llm-cli without --config construct it (f3_cwd_key.py). Both boots shared HOME and the memory keyring, with different cwds: an install dir that has configs/ (the GUI launcher runs cd $INSTALL_DIR), and a project dir with no config (the Claude Code snippet sets no cwd; neither does llm-cli). Results: A config_dir=install/configs and B config_dir=~/.llm-framework, with the same audit.db. 'B verify of untouched log: 1' and 'A verify after B wrote: 2'. Two secrets.store files were created, each with its own audit_hmac_key. The store location was already cwd-dependent before this change, but pairing it with the per-user audit DB, and generating a key silently, is new. The result is false tamper reports on an untouched log. The side claims also hold by code: set_secret returns True even when _save_store swallowed a write error, and _audit_key regenerates the key when get_secret returns None after a decrypt failure.

kept.title: A damaged or unreadable policy file falls back to the recommended defaults, which are looser than a stricter stored policy
kept.failure_scenario: The user sets read=deny and local_write=deny, or denies read_build_log per tool. The file then becomes invalid, for example through an unknown key (extra='forbid'), a hand edit, a newer version's field, or a transient OSError such as EMFILE. PolicyStore.load() returns ToolPolicy() and drops the user's choices. Read tools become ALLOW without any question, and local writes become ASK, so an MCP client with elicitation can start builds again. This contradicts the comment 'must not grant anything'. Nothing warns about the damaged file. The GUI only shows the first-run dialog with defaults filled in, and saving it overwrites the stricter policy for good.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/policy_fallback.py: stored policy gives read_build_log=DENY and start_build=DENY. After adding one unknown key: 'damaged: Decision.ALLOW Decision.ASK configured= False'.
kept.suggested_fix: When the file exists but cannot be read or validated, return a deny-all policy (or ASK for every tier and READ=DENY), log or warn loudly, and keep the damaged file, e.g. as .bad, instead of letting the setup dialog overwrite it silently. Use the recommended defaults only when the file does not exist.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with PolicyStore from 84393cf (f4_policy.py). With all tiers stored as DENY, adding one unknown key (extra='forbid') or version=2 makes load() return ToolPolicy(): read_build_log -> allow, start_build -> ask, configured=False. That contradicts the code's own comment ('must not grant anything'). load() runs on every decide(), so a transient OSError also loosens the policy for that one call. The GUI then opens the first-run dialog pre-filled from registry.policy(), i.e. the defaults, and Save overwrites the stricter file. `mcp serve` only prints 'not set up yet' and never mentions the damage. Severity is lower than claimed: save() is atomic and validated, so damage comes from hand edits, a version downgrade or transient I/O errors, and the loosened tiers are READ=allow and writes=ask (still confirmed by the user).
kept.corrected_fix: Use the recommended defaults only on FileNotFoundError. If the file exists but cannot be read or validated, return a restrictive policy (every tier DENY, or READ and LOCAL_WRITE at ASK with no allows), log a warning naming the file, keep a copy as tool_policy.json.bad, and expose a 'damaged' flag so the GUI, `tools list` and `mcp serve` can tell the user rather than silently pre-filling the defaults.

kept.title: A damaged or unopenable audit.db stops the whole framework from booting (GUI, every CLI command, MCP server)
kept.failure_scenario: build_tool_registry() constructs AuditLog inside FrameworkManager.initialize(), and AuditLog.__init__ runs connect + PRAGMA + CREATE TABLE without any error handling. If ~/.llm-framework/audit.db is corrupt or cannot be opened, for example after a crash or disk-full during a write, a copied DB without its WAL, or a permissions problem, sqlite3.DatabaseError propagates. initialize() then returns False: the GUI shows 'Framework initialization failed' and exits, require_framework() exits 1 for `build start`, `deploy` and the rest, and `mcp serve` cannot start. The message gives no hint that audit.db is the cause. This contradicts the stated principle that 'auditing must never break the call itself'.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/audit_corrupt.py: with audit.db filled with garbage, build_tool_registry raises 'DatabaseError file is not a database'. framework.py:154 calls it inside the try block whose except returns False.
kept.suggested_fix: Open the audit DB lazily or tolerantly. On failure, log an error, move the damaged file aside or set registry.audit to a disabled stub that reports the problem in `tools audit`, and let the framework boot.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with a full boot (f5_corrupt.py). A garbage audit.db gives 'Fatal Error during framework initialization: file is not a database'. A DB cut to its first 4096 bytes gives 'database disk image is malformed'. In both cases initialize() returned False and tool_registry was None. AuditLog.__init__ connects, sets PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and creates the table with no error handling. build_tool_registry runs inside FrameworkManager.initialize's try, whose except returns False. main_window then shows 'Framework initialization failed' and calls sys.exit(1), require_framework() exits 1 for 13 CLI commands, and `mcp serve` cannot start. The message never names audit.db. Corruption is uncommon, but the result is a total outage caused by an optional log, and it contradicts registry._audit's 'auditing must never break the call itself'.

kept.title: MCP records every policy-allowed call as 'approved by the user', and the registry trusts that flag even after the policy changes to ask
kept.failure_scenario: confirm() returns Confirmation(approve=True) whenever the policy decision is ALLOW, and tool() passes approved=True to registry.call(). The audit log, described as a log of 'tool calls and approvals', therefore stores approved=1 for every automatic MCP call, e.g. echo or list_targets with decision=allow, although no human confirmed anything. Because registry.call() treats any approved=True from the caller as a confirmation, a policy that the user tightens from allow to ask between the resolver and the registry decision still lets the call run. The audit then shows decision=ask, approved=1, outcome=ok for a client that cannot even elicit.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/mcp_approved.py uses the real MCP SDK client without elicitation. Audit rows: 'mcp echo decision= allow approved= 1 outcome= ok' and, after the policy changes to ask mid-call, 'mcp write decision= ask approved= 1 outcome= ok' with write is_error False.
kept.suggested_fix: Pass approved only when an elicitation actually happened: return None or a distinct 'not asked' value for ALLOW and DENY. Alternatively, have the resolver return the decision it confirmed and let registry.call() refuse when the current decision is ASK but no real confirmation was obtained.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with the real SDK client and no elicitation (f6_approved.py). A direct registry call (as Ditto will make) is audited as 'decision=allow approved=None'; the same call over MCP is audited as 'decision=allow approved=1', because confirm() returns Confirmation(approve=True) for ALLOW and tool() always passes approved=approval.approve. So the audit says a human approved calls no one confirmed. The opposite also happens: ASK with no elicitation capability is recorded as approved=0 although no one was asked. Nothing in the codebase reads this column yet (`tools audit` does not show it), so the impact is the accuracy of the audit record. Low severity, not medium. The TOCTOU half reproduces only by injecting a policy change between the resolver's decide() and registry.call's decide(). Those two run back to back in one request, and the call was allowed when it was made, so that half is practically irrelevant.
kept.corrected_fix: Forward approved only when an elicitation actually ran. For example, have confirm() return a marker subclass such as PolicyOutcome(Confirmation) for the ALLOW, DENY and no-elicitation paths, and in tool() pass approved=None for that marker and approval.approve otherwise. registry.call then treats ALLOW and DENY on its own, and for ASK without a real answer it denies (approved None, ctx.confirm None). That also fixes the audit columns.

kept.title: Audit verify() does not detect removal of the newest entries (or of all entries), although `--verify` claims it checks that none were removed
kept.failure_scenario: Someone with access to the DB file deletes the latest rows, e.g. the record of a start_build an MCP client ran, or deletes every row. verify() walks only the remaining prefix from GENESIS and returns None, and `llm-cli tools audit --verify` prints 'Audit log intact.' This happens even with the HMAC key, because nothing anchors the chain head or the entry count outside the DB.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/audit_trunc.py: 'after removing the newest entry, verify() -> None' and 'after removing every entry, verify() -> None'. The CLI help says 'Check that no entry was changed or removed'.
kept.suggested_fix: Keep an anchor outside the DB, e.g. the last id and hash, HMAC'd, in user_state_dir or the keyring, updated with each record, and compare against it in verify(). At minimum compare max(id) with sqlite_sequence and report gaps, and correct the help text.
kept.verify_reason: Reproduced with the HMAC key set (f7_trunc.py). Removing the newest row gives verify() -> None while sqlite_sequence still says 4 and 3 rows remain. Removing every row also gives None. Removing a middle row is detected (3). Both the module docstring ('changing or deleting an entry breaks the chain') and the CLI help ('Check that no entry was changed or removed') claim a property the code does not provide: 'Audit log intact.' is printed after the start_build record has been deleted. Low severity: this is an inherent limit of an unanchored chain, so the defect is the false assurance.
kept.corrected_fix: Fix the help text and docstring now, saying that changes and gaps are detected but removal of the newest entries is not. For real detection, keep an anchor outside the DB that is updated on every record(): the last id plus hash, HMAC'd with the audit key, in the keyring or a 0600 file. Compare against it in verify(). A sqlite_sequence/max(id) comparison is only a weak heuristic, because anyone who can edit the DB can also edit sqlite_sequence.

kept.title: Internal pydantic ValidationErrors are treated as user-facing errors: raw text goes unredacted to the client and is never logged
kept.failure_scenario: `except ValueError` is meant for BuildServiceError, but it also catches pydantic ValidationError, which subclasses ValueError. That includes errors from the output-model check and from models built inside handlers, e.g. ArtifactOut from a manifest whose 'created' is a number. The tool fails with pydantic's raw multi-line message, including input_value excerpts and errors.pydantic.dev links. That message reaches the MCP client and the model unredacted (only the audit detail is redacted) and is never logged with a traceback, so a handler or schema bug looks like a user mistake and leaves nothing in the logs.
kept.evidence: scratchpad/review12/valueerror_map.py: the client receives '2 validation errors for ArtifactOut ... input_value={'url': 'https://user:hf_...qrstuvwxyz0123@hf.co/x'} ... input_value=1700000000', and the registry logged nothing.
kept.suggested_fix: Catch pydantic.ValidationError (and TypeError from the output check) before the ValueError branch and treat it as an internal error: logger.error(..., exc_info=True) plus a generic ToolError('<title> failed (internal error)'). Run redact_secrets over every message that reaches the client.
kept.verify_reason: pydantic ValidationError subclasses ValueError, so `except ValueError` (meant for BuildServiceError) catches it. Reproduced in two ways (f8_valerr.py, f8_logcheck.py). (1) A build_info.json with 'created': 1700000000 makes list_artifacts fail for every manifest, and the client gets '1 validation error for ArtifactOut ... input_value=1700000000 ... errors.pydantic.dev'. (2) A handler returning {'x': 5} for a str field gives the raw pydantic text and no log line, while a RuntimeError in a handler is logged with a traceback. Only the redacted audit detail records it. Impact is overstated: manifests the framework writes contain only strings (builder overwrites created/board/format/quantization, build.sh writes strings), so a secret inside a wrongly typed field is unlikely. The generic Exception branch also passes unredacted text to the client, so missing redaction is not specific to this branch. What remains is low-severity misclassification: handler bugs and bad data look like user mistakes and leave no log line.
kept.corrected_fix: In registry.call, catch pydantic.ValidationError (and the TypeError from the output check) before `except ValueError`. Treat it as internal: logger.error(..., exc_info=True), audit it, and raise ToolError(f'{spec.title} failed (internal error)'). Apply redact_secrets to every ToolError message built in call(), including the generic branch. Separately, consider skipping a manifest that fails ArtifactOut validation in list_artifacts so one bad file does not break the whole listing.

kept.title: A cancel can be undone when a later stage resets progress.status, so the build runs to COMPLETED
kept.failure_scenario: The user cancels while the Trivy security scan runs. The scan runs on every build by default and can take minutes; its container is never registered in _active_containers. cancel_build sets CANCELLED and returns True, and the orchestrator/BuildService report 'cancelled'. When the scan ends, _execute_build_modules runs `progress.status = BuildStatus.BUILDING` (_generate_imatrix does the same with CALIBRATING at line 809) and wipes out the CANCELLED. _run_container's _check_cancelled then passes, and the conversion container runs for up to build_timeout. The build ends COMPLETED and writes build_info.json and the golden ZIP, so list_artifacts and the deployment window show the cancelled build as deployable. The same thing happens at line 415 (`prog.status = PREPARING`) for a build cancelled while it waits for an executor thread: cancelling during an image build does not stop that build's thread, but it stops counting toward max_concurrent_builds (line 285 excludes CANCELLED). The next build is then accepted, waits in QUEUED, and if it is cancelled there it is restarted and built in full.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_cancel_scan.py (fake docker client, cancel during the scan): 'status right after cancel: CANCELLED' -> 'status after 2s more: COMPLETED', container events ['start','wait'] with no 'stop', log shows 'Golden Artifact created'. review12/repro_cancel_queued.py: A is cancelled during its image build, so C is accepted and sits in QUEUED; C is cancelled -> CANCELLED, yet the end state is 'A/B/C: CANCELLED COMPLETED COMPLETED' and containers 'llm-build-B', 'llm-build-C' were created.
kept.suggested_fix: Never assign stage statuses unconditionally. Add a helper under self._lock that raises BuildCancelled instead of overwriting CANCELLED, and use it for PREPARING/CALIBRATING/BUILDING. Call _check_cancelled at the start of _execute_build and right after _scan_image_security. Keep counting a cancelled build as active until its worker thread finishes. Ideally cancel_build should also terminate the buildx subprocess and the trivy container.
kept.verify_reason: I reproduced this with a fake docker client against both 84393cf and HEAD (verify-build-service-engine/f1_cancel_scan.py). I cancelled during _scan_image_security: cancel_build returned True and the status read 'cancelled'. When the scan returned, _execute_build_modules set BUILDING, _run_container's _check_cancelled passed, and the llm-build container ran ['start-requested','running','wait','remove'] with no stop. The final status was 'completed' and build_info.json plus Model_Card.md were written. The queued variant reproduces too (f1_cancel_queued.py, max_concurrent_builds=1). A is cancelled during its image build; its thread is still busy, but A no longer counts toward the limit, so C is accepted and sits in QUEUED. C is cancelled, then _execute_build sets PREPARING over CANCELLED, and the end state is A=cancelled, C=completed with container llm-build-C created. In both cases the orchestrator task is already cancelled, so nothing supervises the engine thread, and list_builds/list_artifacts then show the output.
kept.corrected_fix: Route every stage transition (PREPARING, CALIBRATING, BUILDING, and also COMPLETED) through a helper that, under self._lock, raises BuildCancelled if the status is CANCELLED instead of overwriting it. Call _check_cancelled at the start of _execute_build and right after _scan_image_security. Count a build toward max_concurrent_builds until its worker thread has actually returned, for example with a separate 'finished' flag set in a finally block in _execute_build, not by status alone. Optionally keep the buildx Popen and the trivy container per build so that cancel_build can terminate them.

kept.title: BuildService/CLI validation accepts board-specific quantizations when board is omitted, but the container silently builds for rk3588
kept.failure_scenario: An MCP client or Ditto calls start_build(model='org/m', target='Rockchip', format='rkllm', quantization='w4a16') without a board. validate() leaves board=None because RKLLM has two boards. check_request then compares the quantization against the union of all boards (quantizations_for(None)), so w4a16 is accepted. TARGET_BOARD is passed as '', and build.sh/rkllm_module.sh fall back to rk3588 (`BOARD="${TARGET_BOARD:-rk3588}"`). The RKLLM toolkit then rejects w4a16 on rk3588, but only after the image build, the model download and the model load. The same request with board='rk3588' is refused up front. `llm-cli build start -f rkllm -q w4a16` without -b has the identical gap (same logic in cli.py start_build). For RKNN, an omitted board silently produces an rk3588-only .rknn file.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_validate.py against the shipped target.yml: 'rkllm w4a16, board given rk3588 -> refused: Quantization 'w4a16' is not supported for rkllm on rk3588' vs 'rkllm w4a16, no board -> ACCEPTED board=None quant='w4a16'' (also w4a16_g32). targets/Rockchip/modules/build.sh:21 and rkllm_module.sh default the board to rk3588.
kept.suggested_fix: When a format runs on more than one board, require a board, or resolve the effective default board (e.g. a `default_board` capability matching build.sh's rk3588) before calling check_request and pass it explicitly as target_board. Do this in BuildService.validate, in the CLI and in the GUI.
kept.verify_reason: I reproduced this with the real BuildService.validate and the shipped target.yml (f2_f3_validate.py, identical at 84393cf and HEAD). rkllm/w4a16 with board=rk3588 is refused ('not supported for rkllm on rk3588'). rkllm/w4a16 with no board is ACCEPTED with board=None, because quantizations_for(None) returns the union of all boards. _container_env then passes TARGET_BOARD='', and build.sh:21 and rkllm_module.sh:11 fall back to rk3588, a combination the framework itself declares unsupported. cli.py start_build has the same logic at line 547-549. The GUI always selects a board, so it is not affected. The RKNN part, where an omitted board yields an rk3588 .rknn, is a valid combination and only a default; the real defect is the accepted invalid quantization.
kept.corrected_fix: When a format runs on more than one board and no board is given, resolve the board the container will actually use before calling check_request. That is rk3588 today, ideally read from a declared default_board capability that a test keeps in sync with build.sh. Pass it explicitly as target_board, or refuse the request and ask for a board. Apply this in BuildService.validate and in cli.py start_build.

kept.title: check_request refuses IMatrix without a dataset, so the orchestrator's built-in calibration text can never be used (regression for `--imatrix` without `--dataset`)
kept.failure_scenario: `llm-cli build start -m org/m -t Rockchip -q IQ2_XS --imatrix` (no --dataset), the GUI IMatrix checkbox without a chosen file, and start_build(use_imatrix=True) over MCP are all refused with 'IMatrix needs a calibration dataset.' (the CLI exits 2). Before this change set the CLI accepted this and the orchestrator supplied a dataset itself (the `elif req.use_imatrix:` branch in _run_build_pipeline). Commit 0681e20 states 'A GGUF build with IMatrix but no dataset of its own now uses this text', but that branch is unreachable from every entry point. Quantizations listed in needs_imatrix (IQ1_*, IQ2_XXS/XS/S) therefore always require a user-supplied file.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_imatrix.py: check_request('gguf','rk3588','Q4_K_M', dataset=False, imatrix=True) -> ['IMatrix needs a calibration dataset.'] (same for IQ2_XS). GUI builder_tab._submit_build, cli.py start_build and BuildService.validate all call check_request with dataset=bool(user dataset). tests/test_foundation.py:53 enshrines the refusal.
kept.suggested_fix: Drop the `imatrix and not dataset` rule (or apply it only to targets without a default calibration set), since the orchestrator provides the shipped calibration text. Update the test to match.
kept.verify_reason: check_request('gguf', None, 'IQ2_XS', dataset=False, imatrix=True) returns ['IMatrix needs a calibration dataset.']. I ran the real CLI (`build start -m org/m -t Rockchip -q IQ2_XS --imatrix`) from another directory against both 84393cf and HEAD: it prints that message and exits 2. At ab3367a the CLI and GUI accepted --imatrix without a dataset, and the orchestrator's `elif req.use_imatrix:` branch supplied one (Ditto's filler inside the range, the shipped calibration text since 0681e20). The CLI, the GUI _submit_build and BuildService.validate all pass dataset=bool(user dataset), and these are the only callers of submit_build_request. That branch is therefore dead code, and quantizations in needs_imatrix always need a user file.
kept.corrected_fix: Drop the `imatrix and not dataset` rule for formats where the orchestrator supplies a default calibration set (GGUF). Change the needs_imatrix message to 'enable IMatrix' without 'provide a calibration dataset'. Update the test_foundation.py case ('gguf','rk3566','Q4_K_M',{'imatrix':True}) accordingly.

kept.title: Relative output paths now resolve against the installation path, but the CLI deploy commands still look in the working directory, and `-o` changed meaning
kept.failure_scenario: A user runs `llm-cli build start ...` from a project directory, not the install dir. The default output_base_dir 'output/build_TS' (and an explicit `-o ./results`) is now re-anchored to build_engine.base_dir (the installation path), so artifacts land in <install>/output/... or <install>/results/... . The CLI prints 'Output: output/build_TS' or './results', and `llm-cli deploy list-artifacts` / `deploy package NAME` still read Path(ctx.config['output_dir']) relative to the CWD (cli.py:971, 1012). The new build is not listed and cannot be packaged, and a user-chosen relative -o directory no longer means the CWD (unlike --dataset, which the CLI resolves against the CWD). Before this change the orchestrator and builder both used CWD-relative paths, so CLI build and deploy agreed.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_output_dir.py (real LLMOrchestrator, CWD=/tmp/userproject-*): 'output/build_20261010_120000' -> /tmp/install-*/output/build_.../Rockchip/model/Q4_K_M, './results' -> /tmp/install-*/results/..., while 'CLI deploy list-artifacts/deploy package look in: /tmp/userproject-*/output'.
kept.suggested_fix: Resolve user-supplied CLI paths at the CLI boundary (Path(output_dir).resolve() against the CWD) before building the BuildRequest. Make `deploy list-artifacts`/`deploy package` use framework.resolve_path(config output_dir) and list_builds, like BuildService and the GUI deployment window. Alternatively, resolve once in each entry point and stop re-anchoring inside the orchestrator.
kept.verify_reason: I reproduced this with the real LLMOrchestrator, a fake engine with base_dir=<install>, and CWD set to another directory (f4_f5_paths.py, same at 84393cf and HEAD). 'output/build_20261010_120000' resolves to <install>/output/build_.../Rockchip/model/Q4_K_M, and './results' to <install>/results/... . cli.py list-artifacts and deploy package still use Path(ctx.config['output_dir']), which is 'output' relative to the CWD (lines 938/978 at 84393cf, 971/1011 at HEAD). Before the range, the orchestrator used Path(req.output_base_dir) relative to the CWD, so CLI build and CLI deploy agreed. The re-anchoring was added in a1d74f4, and the deploy commands were not updated. A CLI build is not visible to `deploy list-artifacts` unless the CWD is the install dir.
kept.corrected_fix: At the CLI boundary, resolve an explicit -o against the CWD (Path(output_dir).resolve()), as is already done for --dataset. Make the default output dir and `deploy list-artifacts`/`deploy package` use framework.resolve_path(config output_dir), with list_builds as in BuildService and the deployment window. Have the GUI pass framework.resolve_path(...) too, so that every entry point hands the orchestrator an absolute path.

kept.title: output_dir containing '~' is expanded by resolve_path (BuildService, deployment listing) but not by the orchestrator, so GUI/CLI builds go to a literal '~' directory
kept.failure_scenario: With output_dir: ~/llm-builds in the config, GUI builds (builder_tab passes the raw value) and CLI builds land in <install>/~/llm-builds/... because the orchestrator only checks is_absolute() and never expands '~'. BuildService builds land in /home/<user>/llm-builds/... . The deployment window and the list_artifacts tool scan resolve_path(...) = /home/<user>/llm-builds, so every GUI-started build is missing from the deployment window and from MCP list_artifacts. BuildEngine.output_dir has the same literal '~' problem.

kept.title: Any exception from container.wait is reported as a build_timeout expiry
kept.failure_scenario: container.wait can fail long before the timeout: docker.errors.NotFound (container removed externally or by a prune), requests ConnectionError (daemon restarted), or an APIError 500. All of them are turned into 'The cont stage ran longer than 3600 s and was stopped (setting build_timeout)' after a few milliseconds. The real cause only survives in __cause__, which never reaches progress.errors, the CLI/GUI or self-healing. The user, or Ditto's AI analysis, is told to raise build_timeout, and heuristics such as 'No space left on device' can no longer match.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_wait_errors.py: 'NotFound after 0.00s -> TimeoutError: The cont stage ran longer than 3600 s ...', and the same for ConnectionError and APIError.
kept.suggested_fix: Treat only a real read timeout as a timeout: requests ReadTimeout, or a ConnectionError wrapping urllib3 ReadTimeoutError, or elapsed >= timeout. For any other error, still kill and remove the container, but re-raise with the original message.
kept.verify_reason: f6_wait_errors.py calls the real _run_container with container.wait raising docker.errors.NotFound, requests ConnectionError and docker.errors.APIError. Each one became 'TimeoutError: The cont stage ran longer than 3600 s and was stopped (setting build_timeout).' after 0.00 s, at both 84393cf and HEAD. Before the range, the original exception propagated and its message went into progress.errors. Now only __cause__ has it, and that never reaches progress.errors, the CLI/GUI, or self_healing.analyze_error (job.error_log is built from status.errors).
kept.corrected_fix: Record t0 before wait. Report a timeout only if the error is a requests ReadTimeout, a ConnectionError wrapping a urllib3 ReadTimeoutError (unix-socket transport), or if time.monotonic()-t0 >= timeout. Otherwise still kill (best effort), then raise a RuntimeError that includes the original message and the log tail.

kept.title: Cancel while build_model is in the executor leaves an unsupervised build that is never cancelled
kept.failure_scenario: _run_job awaits run_in_executor(build_model) and only appends the id to state.build_ids after that returns. A cancel_request landing during that await sees build_ids without the new id, so cancel_build is never called. task.cancel() then interrupts the await, but the executor thread still submits the build. The build runs to completion with no orchestrator polling it, occupies an engine slot, and writes artifacts, while the request reports 'cancelled'. The same happens for the retry after an applied healing fix.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_orch_cancel.py (fake engine whose build_model takes 0.5 s to widen the window): 'cancel_request -> True | state: cancelled | build_ids: []', 'engine builds: {'r1_001': 'building'} | cancel_build calls: []'.
kept.suggested_fix: Record the build id (job.job_id) in state.build_ids before submitting. Alternatively, after build_model returns, check state.status == CANCELLED and call cancel_build. Shield the executor call so the id is always recorded.
kept.verify_reason: The code path is unambiguous: _run_job awaits run_in_executor(build_model) and appends to state.build_ids only after it returns, and CancelledError (a BaseException) skips the append. f8_orch_cancel.py uses the real LLMOrchestrator with a fake engine whose build_model takes 0.3 s to widen the window. It printed 'cancel_request -> True | state: cancelled | build_ids: []', and later the engine build was 'completed' with no cancel_build calls (84393cf and HEAD). The real window is only as long as build_model plus the executor handoff (about a millisecond). A cancel from the BuildService/MCP thread scheduled in that window hits it, so the severity is low.
kept.corrected_fix: Append job.job_id to state.build_ids before the executor call; build_model returns config.build_id, which is job.job_id. Also, after build_model returns, check whether state.status is CANCELLED and if so call build_engine.cancel_build. Wrapping the executor await in asyncio.shield ensures the follow-up runs even when the task is cancelled.

kept.title: _run_container can miss a cancel that arrives while container.start() is in flight
kept.failure_scenario: _run_container checks for cancellation and then calls container.start(). If cancel_build runs between the check and the daemon actually starting the container, container.stop() hits a created-but-not-running container, which Docker answers with 304 (no-op, no exception). start() then proceeds and the stage runs its full length (up to build_timeout); BuildCancelled is raised only afterwards.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_stop_before_start.py (container fake with Docker's 304 semantics, start latency 0.3 s, cancel at 0.1 s): 'BuildCancelled after 2.3s (stage ran its full 2.0 s)', events ['start-requested','stop (304: not running, no-op)','running','wait','remove'].
kept.suggested_fix: After container.start() returns, check _check_cancelled again and kill the container if the build was cancelled. Alternatively, have cancel_build record a flag that _run_container honours right after start.
kept.verify_reason: There is a real check-then-act gap between _check_cancelled and container.start(), and no re-check after start. The window is much narrower than the finding says, though, and the repro's model of Docker is not accurate. In moby, containerStart holds the container lock for the whole start, and ContainerStop's IsRunning takes the same lock. A stop that arrives while the daemon is already starting the container waits and then stops it normally, so _run_container raises BuildCancelled after wait. The 304 no-op only happens if the stop is processed before the daemon takes the lock, which leaves a window of a few milliseconds (request transit plus ContainerStart pre-checks). I could not reproduce it because Docker is not available. If the race is hit, the stage runs to completion and the build ends CANCELLED without artifacts being blocked earlier.
kept.corrected_fix: After container.start() returns, call _check_cancelled again (or check the status); if the build was cancelled, kill the container and raise BuildCancelled. This closes the window regardless of daemon timing.

kept.title: read_build_log returns every line twice after a healing retry, and the failed attempt's log is gone
kept.failure_scenario: After an approved fix, _heal_and_retry calls _run_job with the same job, so build_id == job.job_id again. The engine replaces the progress object and state.build_ids becomes [id, id]. log_tail iterates both entries and returns each line of the retry twice, which also pushes real lines out of the `lines` window. The log of the attempt whose failure the user approved a fix for is no longer reachable.
kept.evidence: review12/repro_logtail_dup.py: 'build_ids: ['req_..._001', 'req_..._001']', 'log_tail: ['attempt 2 line A', 'attempt 2 line B', 'attempt 2 line A', 'attempt 2 line B']' (attempt 1 lines missing).
kept.suggested_fix: Give retries a distinct build id (e.g. job_id + '_r1'), or de-duplicate state.build_ids. Keep the earlier attempt's progress so log_tail can show both attempts.
kept.verify_reason: f10_logtail.py uses the real LLMOrchestrator and the real BuildService.log_tail, with a fake engine that fails the first attempt, plus an automatic healing proposal that gets approved. The result was build_ids ['req_..._001', 'req_..._001'] and log_tail ['attempt 2 line A', 'attempt 2 line B', 'attempt 2 line A', 'attempt 2 line B'], with the attempt 1 lines gone (84393cf and HEAD). The cause: _heal_and_retry re-runs _run_job with the same job, so build_id == job.job_id; the real BuildEngine.build_model replaces self._builds[build_id]; and _run_job appends the id again.
kept.corrected_fix: Give the retry its own build id (for example f'{job.job_id}_r1' passed into _map_job_to_config), so both progresses are kept and log_tail shows both attempts in order. Alternatively, de-duplicate state.build_ids in _run_job and in log_tail, though that still loses attempt 1.

kept.title: RKLLM request without a board is validated against every board's types, but build.sh builds it for rk3588
kept.failure_scenario: `llm-cli build start -m Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B -t Rockchip -f rkllm -q w4a16` (no --board), or the MCP start_build tool with format=rkllm, quantization=w4a16 and no board. rkllm has two boards, so neither the CLI nor BuildService fills one in. quantizations_for(None) returns the union of both boards' types, so w4a16 passes validation. target_board stays None and TARGET_BOARD is ''. build.sh then defaults BOARD to rk3588, rkllm_module picks PLATFORM=rk3588, and export_rkllm runs `--quant w4a16 --target rk3588`. The target's own capabilities block declares that combination invalid, and the test suite asserts it is refused when the board is given. The build fails late in the container, after the Hugging Face download and model load, instead of being refused up front.
kept.evidence: caps_matrix.py: check_request('rkllm', None, 'w4a16') -> [] while check_request('rkllm','rk3588','w4a16') -> 'not supported for rkllm on rk3588'. cli_repro.py: `-f rkllm -q w4a16` exits 0 and submits target_board=None, quantization_options=['w4a16']. build.sh: BOARD="$(echo "${TARGET_BOARD:-rk3588}" ...)" ; builder._container_env: "TARGET_BOARD": config.target_board or "".

The CLI `-f rkllm -q w4a16` exits 0 and submits target_board=None, quantization_options=['w4a16'] (cli_repro.py). BuildService.validate accepts it with board=None (bs_verify.py). builder._container_env sets TARGET_BOARD to '', and both build.sh and rkllm_module.sh use ${TARGET_BOARD:-rk3588}, which also replaces an empty value. So export_rkllm gets --quant w4a16 --target rk3588, a combination the target's own capabilities and test_foundation declare invalid. The container failure itself could not be run because Docker is down. Note this is not a regression: before the range the same request also failed late. It is a correctness gap in the new validation, which treats board=None as 'any board' while the build resolves None to rk3588. The GUI is not affected because it always sends a board.
kept.corrected_fix: In check_request, when board is None and the format has board_quantizations, either require a board ('rkllm needs --board: rk3588, rk3576') or validate against the types that are allowed on every board of that format. Apply this in the CLI and BuildService/MCP. Alternatively declare a default board in the capabilities and both validate against it and pass it on as target_board, so validation and build.sh agree.

kept.title: CLI `build start --board` is now case-sensitive: uppercase board names that used to work are rejected

BuildService.validate (MCP/Ditto) lowercases the board, while the CLI passes it unchanged to check_request.
